text: Microsoft Corporation, a technology company incorporated in the State of Washington with IRS identification number 91-1144442 and headquartered at One Microsoft Way, Redmond, Washington 98052-6399, filed an annual report on Form 10-K pursuant to Section 13 or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2016. The company’s Commission File Number is 001-37845. As of December 31, 2015, the aggregate market value of Microsoft’s common stock held by non-affiliates was $424.5 billion based on the closing sale price on the NASDAQ National Market System. As of July 25, 2016, there were 7,792,515,573 shares of common stock outstanding. Microsoft’s vision is to empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more, with a strategy focused on building best-in-class platforms and productivity services for a mobile-first, cloud-first world. The company operates globally in over 190 countries and offers a wide range of software products, services, and devices, including operating systems, cross-device productivity applications, server applications, business solutions, desktop and server management tools, software development tools, video games, and training and certification services. It also designs, manufactures, and sells devices such as PCs, tablets, gaming consoles, phones, and intelligent devices that integrate with its cloud-based offerings. Microsoft provides cloud-based solutions, solution support, consulting services, and delivers relevant online advertising to a global audience. Its research and development efforts are centered on three interconnected ambitions: reinventing productivity and business processes, building the intelligent cloud platform, and creating more personal computing. In reinventing productivity, Microsoft enhances customer experiences through tools like Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, OneNote, OneDrive, Skype, and Microsoft Dynamics (Dynamics), offering these as cloud services via Office 365 for access across devices and locations. The company believes it is one of two leaders in the cloud market, leveraging economies of scale in datacenters to reduce costs, improve resource utilization, and lower maintenance labor costs through multi-tenancy. Microsoft’s cloud services, including Azure, SQL Server, Windows Server, Visual Studio, System Center, and Azure, provide a public, private, and hybrid cloud platform capable of supporting modern business needs. It enables enterprises to combine existing datacenters with public cloud infrastructure for unified security, management, and administration. Microsoft also offers identity and directory services, rich data storage and analytics, machine learning, media, web and mobile backend services, and developer productivity tools. To support a rich developer ecosystem, the platform is designed to be extensible. In creating more personal computing, Microsoft focuses on user-centered experiences through Windows 10, launched in July 2015, which serves as a service that powers a full spectrum of devices, offering features such as Cortana, Windows Hello, Windows Ink, Microsoft Edge, and universal applications. The company aims to expand economic opportunity through an OEM ecosystem, first-party premium device portfolio, and monetization via services, subscriptions, gaming, and search advertising. Microsoft is investing in new input/output methods such as speech, pen, gesture, and augmented reality holograms. The company’s future opportunities include delivering new productivity and business processes, building cloud-based services, establishing the Windows platform across servers and devices and the cloud, developing devices with natural interaction methods, and applying machine learning to make technology more intuitive and responsive to user needs. Microsoft’s operating segments, as of fiscal year 2016, are Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, and More Personal Computing, reflecting a reorganization aligned with its strategic direction. The Productivity and Business Processes segment includes Office Commercial (offering volume licensing and Office 365 commercial subscriptions for products like Office, Exchange, SharePoint, and Skype for Business, along with related Client Access Licenses), Office Consumer (offering retail and consumer subscription access to Office and services such as Skype, Outlook.com, and OneDrive), and Dynamics business solutions (including Dynamics ERP, on-premises and online CRM). This segment is designed to increase personal, team, and organizational productivity through a range of products and services, with growth dependent on reaching new users, adding value to core offerings, and expanding into new markets such as security, analytics, and collaboration. Additional segment and geographic details are provided in Note 21 – Segment Information and Geographic Data of the Notes to Financial Statements.

Product information is detailed in Note 21 – Segment Information and Geographic Data of the Notes to Financial Statements (Part II, Item 8 of this Form 10-K). The company’s reportable segments are as follows: Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, More Personal Computing, and Dynamics. The Productivity and Business Processes segment includes Office Commercial, Office Consumer, and Dynamics business solutions. Office Commercial offers products and services to enhance personal, team, and organizational productivity and includes volume licensing, Software Assurance, and subscriptions to Office 365 commercial for products such as Office, Exchange, SharePoint, and Skype for Business, along with Client Access Licenses (“CALs”). Office Consumer focuses on personal productivity and includes Office sold through retail or Office 365 consumer subscriptions, as well as Office Consumer Services like Skype, Outlook.com, and OneDrive, with revenue driven by new device purchases and the shift to Office 365, as well as demand for communication and storage through subscriptions, advertising, and minute sales. Skype connects users across devices. Dynamics provides business solutions for financial management, CRM, supply chain, and analytics for small and mid-sized businesses and large organizations, with revenue primarily driven by the number of information workers licensed. The Intelligent Cloud segment includes server products and cloud services such as SQL Server, Windows Server, Visual Studio, System Center, related CALs, and Azure, as well as Enterprise Services like Premier Support Services and Microsoft Consulting Services. Server products support IT professionals and developers with integrated infrastructure, middleware, and development tools, with revenue influenced by volume licensing, OEM sales, and retail products; CALs provide access to SQL Server and Windows Server. Azure is a scalable cloud platform offering computing, networking, storage, databases, analytics, and enterprise mobility solutions, enabling developers to build and manage applications across platforms without managing underlying infrastructure. Enterprise Services assist in deploying and managing Microsoft solutions and provide training and certification. The More Personal Computing segment includes Windows, Devices, Gaming, and Search Advertising. Windows delivers a consistent experience across devices, with revenue impacted by OEM licensing, device form factor, market demand differences, customer mix, inventory levels, pricing changes, and piracy; volume licensing is driven by commercial demand and Software Assurance and the number of information workers. Patent licensing covers a range of technologies, including mobile and cloud; Windows Embedded extends Windows and cloud capabilities to intelligent systems. Devices include Microsoft Surface, phones, and PC accessories; Surface Pro 4 and Surface Book were released in October 2015; after acquiring Nokia’s Devices and Services business in April 2014, Microsoft began manufacturing Lumia phones and announced plans in July 2015 to restructure its phone business, further streamlining its smartphone hardware in May 2016, and selling its entry-level feature phone business in May 2016, with the transaction expected to close in the second half of 2016 subject to regulatory approvals. Gaming includes Xbox 360 (released November 2005), Xbox One (November 2013), Xbox One S (August 2016), and the Windows 10 Xbox app (July 2015); Xbox Live enables online gaming experiences accessible on consoles, Windows devices, and other platforms, including subscriptions, content sales, and advertising, and the business benefits from exclusive content, device reliability, and online services. The acquisition of Mojang Synergies AB in November 2014 added Minecraft to the gaming portfolio. Search Advertising, including Bing and Bing Ads, delivers relevant online ads and grows through attracting new users, understanding user intent, and matching it with content and advertiser offerings. Competitors include Adobe, Apple, Cisco, Facebook, Google, IBM, Oracle, SAP, and local developers in Asia and Europe; Skype for Business and Skype compete with instant messaging, voice, and video providers; Dynamics competes with Oracle and SAP for large organizations and with Infor, The Sage Group, and NetSuite for small and mid-sized businesses; Salesforce.com competes directly with Dynamics CRM on-premises and CRM Online. Server products face competition from Hewlett-Packard, IBM, Oracle, and Linux-based systems, with open-source software like Apache, MySQL, PHP, and Eclipse competing in web platforms and middleware; database, BI, and data warehousing solutions compete with IBM, Oracle, SAP; system management solutions compete with BMC, CA Technologies, Hewlett-Packard, IBM, and VMware; software development tools compete with Adobe, IBM, Oracle, and open-source projects like Eclipse, PHP, and Ruby on Rails; Azure competes with Amazon, Google, IBM, Oracle, Salesforce.com, VMware, and open-source offerings, with advantages including hybrid cloud deployment and scalability; Enterprise Services compete with multinational consulting firms and niche technology providers. Operations centers support order processing, credit, information processing, and logistics in Ireland (for Europe, Middle East, Africa), Singapore (for Japan, India, Greater China, Asia-Pacific), and in Fargo, North Dakota, Fort Lauderdale, Florida, Puerto Rico, Redmond, Washington, and Reno, Nevada (for Latin America and North America); datacenters are located in the Americas, Australia, Europe, and Asia. Products are localized for international markets to reflect local languages and conventions, modifying interfaces, dialog boxes, and translating text. Phone manufacturing is primarily in Vietnam, and the entry-level feature phone business, including the Vietnam facility, was sold in May 2016. Devices other than phones are manufactured by third-party contract manufacturers, with the ability to switch vendors if needed. Research and development expenses were $12.0 billion in fiscal years 2016 and 2015, and $11.4 billion in 2014, representing 14% and 13% of revenue in 2016 and 2015, respectively, and 13% in 2014; the company plans to continue significant investments in R&D. Products and services are developed internally through three engineering groups: Applications and Services Engineering Group (productivity, communication, education, search), Cloud and Enterprise Engineering Group (cloud infrastructure, server, database, CRM, ERP, development tools), and Windows and Devices Engineering Group (Windows across devices, hardware, online marketplaces). Internal development supports product differentiation, technical control, and timely implementation of enhancements based on usage patterns and hardware advances; before releasing new platforms, the company provides vendors with resources, guidelines, training, and testing, and creates internal product documentation. Intellectual property is protected through enforcement of copyright, trademark, trade secret, and other rights in the U.S. and internationally, with the company holding over 61,000 U.S. and international patents issued and over 35,000 patents pending.

Microsoft offers enterprise resource planning, management, development tools, and other business process applications and services for enterprises. The Windows and Devices Engineering Group focuses on the Windows platform across all device types, hardware development, and associated online marketplaces. Internal development enables Microsoft to maintain competitive advantages through product differentiation and tighter technical control, allowing the company to decide which modifications and enhancements to implement and when. Microsoft strives to gather early insights into changing usage patterns and hardware advancements that may impact software design. Before launching new software platforms, the company provides application vendors with resources, guidelines, training, and testing support, and generally creates product documentation internally. Microsoft protects its intellectual property through active enforcement of copyright, trademark, trade secret, and other rights in the U.S. and internationally. It is a leader in patenting, holding over 61,000 U.S. and international patents issued and over 35,000 pending. Much of the internally developed intellectual property is used exclusively in Microsoft products and services, and the company engages in outbound and inbound licensing of specific patented technologies. It also enters into broader cross-license agreements with other technology companies and purchases or licenses technology for incorporation into its products and services. Occasionally, Microsoft makes select intellectual property available at no or low cost to achieve strategic goals such as promoting industry standards, advancing interoperability, or supporting its external development community. While future licenses for various aspects of its products and business methods may be necessary, Microsoft believes such licenses can generally be obtained on commercially reasonable terms based on past experience and industry practice, and that its research and product development are not materially dependent on any single third-party license or agreement. Microsoft’s success is based on creating new and compelling products, services, and experiences, embracing disruptive technology trends, entering new geographic and product markets, and driving broad adoption. The company invests in emerging technology trends and breakthroughs in areas such as digital work and life experiences, cloud computing, and device operating systems and hardware. While its main research and development facilities are in Redmond, Washington, it also operates in Canada, China, Denmark, Finland, France, India, Ireland, Israel, Japan, and the United Kingdom. Corporate-level funding supports long-term research beyond immediate product needs, and business segment-level research is coordinated and leveraged across the company. In addition, Microsoft Research, one of the world’s largest computer science research organizations, collaborates with top universities to advance computer science and gain insights into future technology trends. Microsoft markets and distributes its products and services through OEMs, distributors and resellers, online channels, and Microsoft retail stores. Its sales force works with enterprises and public sector organizations worldwide to identify software needs, manages OEM relationships, and supports solution integrators, independent software vendors, and other partners. OEMs pre-install Microsoft software on devices and servers they sell; the largest component is the Windows operating system. Direct OEMs, such as Acer, ASUST, Dell, Fujitsu, Hewlett-Packard, Lenovo, Samsung, Toshiba, and many regional and local OEMs, have direct agreements with Microsoft. Lower-volume PC manufacturers, or system builders, source software primarily through the Microsoft distributor channel. Distributors and resellers include Ingram Micro, Tech Data, CDW, Dell, Insight Enterprises, and Software House International. LSPs serve large organizations, distributors primarily resell to VARs, and VARs typically reach small- and medium-sized organizations. ESAs are authorized as LSPs and offer services for licensing programs like Select Plus and Open. Microsoft Dynamics is licensed through a global network of channel partners providing vertical solutions and specialized services. Retail packaged products are distributed through independent non-exclusive distributors, authorized replicators, resellers, and retail outlets, with individual consumers primarily obtaining them through retail outlets and Microsoft retail stores. Devices are distributed through third-party retailers and Microsoft retail stores, and phones are distributed via global wireless communications carriers. The company has a network of field sales representatives and support personnel who solicit orders and provide training and sales support. Online, Microsoft delivers commercial cloud-based solutions such as Office 365, Azure, and Dynamics CRM Online, and provides online content services through Bing, MSN portals, Office 365, Xbox Live, Outlook.com, OneDrive, Skype, and the Windows Store. It also offers an online advertising platform, Microsoft Developer Network content, periodic product updates, and technical and practice readiness resources for partners. Cloud-based services are sold through enterprise agreements and new sales programs reach small and medium-sized businesses, including direct sales, partner advisor-supported sales, and resale through operator channels such as telephone, cell, and cable providers. Products are also sold through Microsoft retail stores and online marketplaces. Licensing options include Enterprise Agreement Licensing, which is designed for medium- and large-sized organizations to standardize on a common IT platform, offering perpetual or subscription licenses with Software Assurance and support, typically for three years. The Microsoft Products and Services Agreement (MPSA) allows customers to purchase online services, software licenses, and Software Assurance under a single agreement, with terms up to three years, and Microsoft plans to expand it in fiscal year 2017. Select Plus is designed for medium- and large-sized organizations, allowing perpetual or subscription licenses with Software Assurance (typically up to three years), and includes online services; however, in July 2014, Microsoft announced the retirement of Select Plus over a two-year period, with no new agreements signed after July 2015 and no new orders accepted after July 2016, with the entire business expected to transition to MPSA within a few years. Open Licensing is designed for small- and medium-sized organizations, allowing perpetual or subscription licenses with rights to future versions (typically two or three years), with options to acquire licenses only or with Software Assurance, and renew Software Assurance upon expiration of existing agreements. Open Value and Open Value Subscription offer perpetual or subscription licenses over three years. The Microsoft Online Subscription Agreement enables small and medium-sized businesses to purchase cloud-based services on a monthly or annual basis. Partner programs include the Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider program, which allows partners to manage their entire cloud customer lifecycle with dedicated tools and package their own tools and services into a single monthly or annual bill; the Microsoft Services Provider License Agreement, which enables service providers and independent software vendors to offer software services and hosted applications with three-year terms and monthly consumption-based billing; the Microsoft Online Services Reseller Agreement, which allows partners to bundle Microsoft online services with their own; and the Independent Software Vendor Royalty program, which allows partners to use Microsoft software in their own products. Customers include individual consumers, small- and medium-sized organizations, large global enterprises, public sector institutions, Internet service providers, application developers, and OEMs. No individual customer sales accounted for more than 10% of revenue in fiscal years 2016, 2015, or 2014. Products are shipped promptly upon receipt of purchase orders, so backlog is not significant. As of July 28, 2016, the executive officers were: Satya Nadella (48), Chief Executive Officer; Christopher C. Capossela (46), Executive Vice President and Chief Marketing Officer; Jean-Philippe Courtois (55), Executive Vice President and President, Microsoft Global Sales, Marketing and Operations; Kathleen T. Hogan (50), Executive Vice President, Human Resources; Amy E. Hood (44), Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer; Margaret L. Johnson (54), Executive Vice President, Business Development; and Bradford L. Smith (57), President and Chief Legal Officer. Satya Nadella was appointed CEO in February 2014, previously serving as Executive Vice President, Cloud and Enterprise since July 2013, President, Server and Tools from 2011 to 2013, and Senior Vice President, Online Services Division from 2009 to 2011. Christopher Capossela was appointed Chief Marketing Officer in March 2014, previously leading Consumer Channels Group and holding various marketing leadership roles in the Microsoft Office Division. Jean-Philippe Courtois was named Executive Vice President and President, Microsoft Global Sales, Marketing and Operations in July 2016, previously serving as President of Microsoft International since June 2005 and Chief Executive Officer of Microsoft Europe, Middle East, and Africa since March 2003. Kathleen Hogan was appointed Executive Vice President, Human Resources in November 2014, previously serving as Corporate Vice President of Microsoft Services and Customer Service and Support, joining Microsoft in 2003. Amy Hood was appointed Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer in July 2013, having served as Chief Financial Officer since May 2013, and previously held finance roles in the Business Division and corporate finance. Margaret Johnson was appointed Executive Vice President, Business Development in September 2014, having spent 24 years at Qualcomm in leadership roles, most recently as Executive Vice President of Qualcomm Technologies, Inc., and also serves on the Board of Directors of Live Nation Entertainment, Inc. Bradford Smith was appointed President and Chief Legal Officer in September 2015, previously serving as Executive Vice President, General Counsel, and Secretary since 2011, and as Senior Vice President, General Counsel, and Secretary from 2001 to 2011, and also serves on the Board of Directors of Netflix, Inc. As of June 30, 2016, Microsoft employed approximately 114,000 people full-time, with 63,000 in the U.S. and 51,000 internationally. Of these, 38,000 were in operations (manufacturing, distribution, product support, consulting), 37,000 in product research and development, 29,000 in sales and marketing, and 10,000 in general and administration. Certain employees are subject to collective bargaining agreements. In June 2015, management approved a restructuring plan that eliminated approximately 7,400 positions in fiscal year 2016, primarily in the phone hardware business. In the fourth quarter of 2016, additional restructuring plans were approved, resulting in job eliminations, primarily in the smartphone hardware business and global sales. In addition to 1,850 positions eliminated in May 2016, approximately 2,850 roles globally were reduced during the year.

On March 30, 2016, Microsoft employed approximately 114,000 people on a full-time basis, with 63,000 in the United States and 51,000 internationally. Of these employees, 38,000 were in operations, including manufacturing, distribution, product support, and consulting services; 37,000 in product research and development; 29,000 in sales and marketing; and 10,000 in general and administration. Certain employees are subject to collective bargaining agreements. In June 2015, management approved a restructuring plan that eliminated approximately 7,400 positions in fiscal year 2016, primarily in the phone hardware business. In the fourth quarter of 2016, management approved additional restructuring plans that would result in job eliminations, primarily in the smartphone hardware business and global sales. In addition to the 1,850 positions eliminated in May 2016, approximately 2,850 roles globally were to be reduced during the year as an extension of the earlier plan, with these actions expected to be completed by the end of fiscal year 2017. Microsoft’s Internet address is www.microsoft.com, and its Investor Relations website, www.microsoft.com/investor, provides free access to a variety of information for investors, including annual reports on Form 10-K, quarterly reports on Form 10-Q, current reports on Form 8-K, and amendments to those reports as soon as reasonably practicable after filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The site also includes information on business strategies, financial results, and metrics; announcements of investor conferences, speeches, and events with archives; press releases on quarterly earnings, product and service announcements, legal developments, and international news; corporate governance information such as articles of incorporation, bylaws, governance guidelines, committee charters, codes of conduct and ethics, global corporate social responsibility initiatives, and other governance-related policies; and other news and announcements. Investors are also encouraged to review information posted on social media channels listed on the Investor Relations website. The information on the website is not part of any report filed or furnished to the SEC. Microsoft’s operations and financial results are subject to various risks, including intense competition across all markets for its products and services, which may lead to lower revenue or operating margins. Competitors range from diversified global companies with significant R&D resources to small, specialized firms with narrow product lines, and barriers to entry in many of its businesses are low, with rapid technological change and shifting user needs. Microsoft faces competition from firms with competing platforms, applications, and services, including vertically-integrated models that control both software and hardware, which can reduce Microsoft’s operating margins. Revenue from Windows operating system licenses on personal computers is challenged by competing platforms on smartphones and tablets, which users increasingly use for functions once performed by PCs, potentially reducing developer interest in Windows and affecting margins. Competing platforms have large application marketplaces with significant installed bases, and Microsoft must attract developers to create high-quality, appealing applications for its marketplace, which may increase costs and reduce margins. Competitors also use free applications, online services, and advertising revenue models, which directly compete with Microsoft’s revenue-generating products. Some companies use open source models, distributing software at nominal cost and earning revenue from advertising or complementary services, and some of these firms develop software that mimics Microsoft’s products. The increasing focus on cloud-based services presents execution and competitive risks, as competitors rapidly develop and deploy cloud services, and Microsoft must continue to deliver compelling cloud experiences, maintain compatibility and performance across devices, enhance developer appeal, ensure reliability and data security, and make services platform-agnostic. Microsoft’s significant investments in new products and services, including the Windows operating system, Office, Bing, Windows Phone, Windows Server, the Windows Store, Microsoft Azure, Office 365, and hardware like PCs, tablets, and gaming devices, are speculative and may not achieve expected returns. The launch of Windows 10 with free upgrades to Windows 7 and 8.1 was the most ambitious update effort in the company’s history, with extensive compatibility testing conducted; however, a negative user experience or public backlash could harm market reception and lead to litigation or regulatory actions. Windows 10 also enables new post-license monetization opportunities, and failure to realize these could negatively impact revenue. Data collection practices in Windows 10 could result in regulatory scrutiny, fines, negative public reaction, and reduced product design flexibility. Developing new technologies is complex and can involve long development periods and significant delays or problems, which could adversely affect revenue. Acquisitions, joint ventures, and strategic alliances may have adverse effects; for example, in June 2016, Microsoft announced the acquisition of LinkedIn for approximately $26.2 billion, which involves risks such as failure to advance business strategy, unsatisfactory returns, integration difficulties, or management distraction. These arrangements may also face early termination or renegotiation and may take longer than expected to realize benefits, which could negatively affect operating results. If goodwill or amortizable intangible assets become impaired, Microsoft may be required to record significant charges to earnings. Goodwill is tested at least annually, and impairment may be triggered by a decline in stock price, reduced future cash flow estimates, or slower industry growth. For example, in the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2015, Microsoft recorded a $5.1 billion charge for goodwill impairment and a $2.2 billion charge for intangible asset impairment, and in the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2016, a $480 million charge for intangible asset impairment, both related to the phone business. The LinkedIn acquisition will significantly increase goodwill and intangible asset balances. Microsoft may not earn expected revenues from its intellectual property rights due to difficulties in protecting them globally, especially in countries with weaker intellectual property laws, which could slow revenue growth in those markets. Changes in law may weaken the ability to prevent use of patented technology or collect royalties from licensing, and licensees may fail to pay royalties or contest their obligations. Royalty revenues may decline due to technological evolution, price changes, or difficulty in identifying infringements. Third parties may claim that Microsoft infringes their intellectual property, leading to potential royalty or licensing agreements on less favorable terms, product discontinuation or redesign, or payment of damages, which could reduce operating margins. In some jurisdictions, such as Germany, injunctions can be issued before full litigation of patent validity. Microsoft has paid significant amounts to settle claims and acquire intellectual property to manage this risk and may continue to do so. Unauthorized disclosure of source code could result in loss of trade secret protection, enable third parties to copy functionality, and increase security risks. Cyber-attacks and security vulnerabilities pose threats to Microsoft’s information technology, including from individual hackers, groups, and state-sponsored organizations, who may deploy malicious software, use social engineering, or otherwise attack products, services, networks, and data centers.

There is an unauthorized disclosure of source code, which consists of the detailed program commands for Microsoft’s operating systems and other software programs, a critical component of the company’s business. While portions of the source code are licensed to third parties, Microsoft takes significant steps to protect the secrecy of large portions of its source code. A significant leak could result in the loss of future trade secret protection, make it easier for third parties to copy product functionality, and negatively impact revenue and operating margins. Such a disclosure also increases security risks. Cyber-attacks and security vulnerabilities pose threats to Microsoft’s information technology, including actions by individual hackers, groups, and state-sponsored organizations that may use malicious software, social engineering, or coordinated attacks like distributed denial of service. These threats are constantly evolving, making detection and defense more difficult, and can have cascading effects across internal systems, partner, and customer networks. Breaches could disrupt internal operations, impair service delivery, compromise confidential business information, delay product development, lead to theft or misuse of intellectual property, require increased spending on security technologies, and harm the company’s competitive position. As Microsoft adopts new devices and technologies, including consumer-oriented tools like social networking, its internal policies and security controls may not keep pace with emerging threats. Security of Microsoft’s products, services, and customers’ data is vital, especially since customers relying on cloud-based services depend on the security of Microsoft’s infrastructure. Hackers often target popular operating systems and services, and security is a key factor in customer purchasing decisions. To defend against threats, Microsoft must continuously engineer more secure products, enhance security features, improve software update deployment, develop mitigation technologies, maintain digital security infrastructure, and provide customers with tools like firewalls and anti-virus software. These efforts may reduce operating margins; failure to adequately address security issues could damage the company’s reputation, reduce or delay customer purchases, or lead customers to use competing products, especially if they fail to update systems or install security patches, which could harm revenue. Actual or perceived vulnerabilities may lead to liability claims, and although license agreements typically limit liability, these provisions are not guaranteed to hold up in legal challenges. Legislative or regulatory actions in these areas could increase development and security costs. Disclosure of personal data could lead to liability, reputational harm, and legal exposure, especially as cloud-based offerings grow and more personally identifiable information is stored and processed. Despite security efforts, improper disclosure of customer data remains possible due to gaps in employee or vendor training and security practices. Government authorities may require the production of customer data in response to legal orders, and Microsoft advocates for transparency and appropriate limits on such requests. Perceptions that personal data is not adequately protected could inhibit sales and limit adoption of cloud solutions. Additional security measures or constraints on datacenter operations due to customer expectations or government rules may increase operating expenses. Outages, data losses, and service disruptions could occur if Microsoft fails to maintain adequate operations infrastructure, especially as user traffic, service growth, and product complexity increase. The company invests heavily in datacenters and network infrastructure to support services like Bing, Exchange Online, Office 365, SharePoint Online, OneDrive, Skype, Xbox Live, Microsoft Azure, Outlook.com, Windows Stores, and Microsoft Account services, as well as third-party platform hosting. Maintaining and expanding this infrastructure is expensive and complex, requiring robust and reliable internet connectivity under evolving regulatory and competitive constraints. Inefficiencies or failures, including data loss or connectivity issues, could reduce product quality, damage reputation, and lead to contractual liability or loss of users and advertisers. Microsoft faces scrutiny under U.S. and foreign competition laws, with increased regulatory focus in regions like the EU, the U.S., and China. For example, in 2004, the European Commission required Microsoft to create Windows versions without certain multimedia features and provide specifications for competitors to implement proprietary protocols. In 2009, the Commission accepted commitments to address web browsing interoperability concerns, which expired in 2014. Remaining obligations may limit innovation in Windows, reduce developer appeal, and increase development costs. Availability of licenses for protocols and file formats may allow competitors to create software that mimics Microsoft’s products, reducing sales. Microsoft’s first-party devices and OEM partner devices create both cooperation and competition, raising risks of non-compliance with competition rules, especially in jurisdictions like China. Enforcement of competition laws in these regions is still developing and unpredictable. Government actions or court decisions could require Microsoft to withdraw products from certain markets, develop alternative versions, limit licensing terms, or face precedent-setting rulings. Ongoing commitments from court orders or consent decrees could result in litigation costs, fines, or remedial actions if not met. These actions may also limit monetization opportunities from Windows 10 post-sale. Microsoft’s global operations are subject to anti-corruption laws like the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, which prohibit corrupt payments by employees, vendors, or agents. The company receives inquiries and reports about compliance, particularly in non-U.S. operations, and has cooperated with U.S. authorities. Despite robust compliance programs, violations could result in fines, criminal sanctions, business restrictions, and reputational damage. Geopolitical instability and changes in trade protection laws, sanctions, or regulatory requirements may affect operations in certain regions and expose the company to legal liability and reputational harm if it violates U.S. sanctions on countries like Iran, North Korea, Cuba, Sudan, and Syria. Regulatory areas such as user privacy, telecommunications, data storage, and online content may apply to products like Skype, with enforcement approaches varying by jurisdiction and evolving over time. Compliance may involve significant costs or require changes in products or practices that reduce revenue. Noncompliance could lead to penalties or orders to cease operations. Laws governing personal data handling may hinder service adoption or result in increased costs, legal claims, or fines. For instance, in October 2015, the European Court of Justice invalidated the EU/U.S. safe harbor framework, which allowed data transfers from the EU to the U.S., and its reasoning could be used to challenge other data transfer methods. A new trans-Atlantic agreement, a revised EU data protection directive, or individual member state regulations may emerge, potentially creating burdensome or inconsistent requirements for data location and movement, increasing costs, reducing efficiency, or making it harder to compete with foreign firms. Failure to comply with such rules could result in significant penalties. Microsoft’s business depends on attracting and retaining talented employees, as the industry is highly competitive and international recruitment is limited by domestic immigration laws. Ineffective recruitment or failure to retain key personnel could hinder product development and delivery. Effective succession planning is essential to ensure smooth transitions and strategic execution. Employment laws may also increase operating costs and reduce flexibility in workforce management. The company faces various claims and lawsuits arising from product launches, business transactions, or employment practices. Adverse outcomes could result in substantial damages or injunctive relief, affecting business operations. These claims are subject to uncertainty, and a material adverse impact on financial statements could occur when an unfavorable outcome becomes probable and estimable. Microsoft also faces potential tax liabilities due to income taxes in the U.S. and many foreign jurisdictions, where significant judgment is required in tax calculations. Ongoing audits and economic pressures to increase tax revenue may make favorable tax outcomes more difficult. Although current tax estimates are reasonable, final audit or litigation results could differ materially from historical provisions, affecting financial statements. A significant portion of operating income comes from outside the U.S., and repatriating foreign-held funds could increase effective tax rates. Proposals in Congress to change U.S. tax laws on foreign earnings could materially impact tax expenses and cash flows. Hardware and software products may experience quality or supply issues. Vertically-integrated products like Xbox consoles, Surface devices, phones, and others are complex and can have design, manufacturing, or software defects. Failure to detect or address such issues could lead to significant expenses, lost revenue, and reputational harm. Some components are sourced from sole suppliers, and demand from competitors may limit availability. Delays or unavailability from such suppliers could disrupt sales, and component shortages, excess inventory, or price reductions could increase cost of revenue. Supply chain disruptions in Asia and other regions could affect hardware availability and revenue. Software products may also contain bugs or defects not detected in pre-release testing, leading to reduced sales, reputational damage, repair costs, product delays, or legal liability. Although license agreements typically limit liability, these provisions are not guaranteed to withstand legal challenges. Microsoft strives to empower all people and organizations to achieve more and ensure accessibility of its products.

Hardware components can impact the available capacity, and if a component from a sole-source supplier is delayed or becomes unavailable due to supplier capacity constraints or industry shortages, timely replacement supplies may not be obtained, leading to reduced sales. Component shortages, excess or obsolete inventory, or price reductions resulting in inventory adjustments can increase the cost of revenue. Xbox consoles, Surface devices, phones, and other hardware are assembled in Asia and other regions, where supply chain disruptions may occur, affecting revenue and operating margins. These risks also apply to any other vertically-integrated hardware and software products offered. Software products may contain bugs or defects that interfere with intended operation, and undetected issues in pre-release testing could result in reduced sales, damage to reputation, repair costs, delays in product releases, or legal liability. Although license agreements typically include provisions limiting or eliminating liability, there is no guarantee these provisions will withstand legal challenges. The company strives to empower all people and organizations to achieve more, with accessibility being a key aspect of this mission. Microsoft is a technology company with a mission to empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more. Its strategy focuses on building best-in-class platforms and productivity services for a mobile-first, cloud-first world. The company generates revenue through licensing and supporting software products, offering cloud-based services to consumers and businesses, designing and selling devices that integrate with its cloud services, and delivering online advertising to a global audience. Major expenses include employee compensation, product and service development, marketing, datacenter costs for cloud services, and income taxes. In fiscal year 2016, Microsoft focused on transforming its organization to support this strategy, achieving product development milestones, implementing organizational changes, and making strategic moves to advance three central ambitions: reinventing productivity and business processes, building the intelligent cloud platform, and creating more personal computing. Key highlights from fiscal year 2016 include a commercial cloud annualized revenue run rate exceeding $12.1 billion, Office 365 Consumer subscribers reaching 23.1 million, Dynamics CRM Online seat additions more than doubling year-over-year, Azure revenue growing 113% with compute and SQL database usage more than doubling, enterprise mobility customers nearly doubling to over 33,000, Windows 10 being active on over 350 million devices worldwide, and Xbox Live monthly active users increasing 33% year-over-year to 49 million. In June 2016, Microsoft entered into a definitive agreement to acquire LinkedIn for $196 per share in an all-cash transaction valued at $26.2 billion, inclusive of LinkedIn’s net cash, with the transaction primarily financed through new indebtedness. The Merger Agreement was unanimously approved by the boards of directors of both companies and is expected to close in calendar year 2016, subject to shareholder approval, regulatory clearances, and customary closing conditions. The acquisition is anticipated to accelerate growth in LinkedIn, Office 365, and Dynamics. In May 2016, Microsoft announced the sale of its entry-level feature phone business for $350 million, expected to close in the second half of 2016, subject to regulatory approvals and other conditions. In July 2015, Microsoft announced a plan to restructure its phone business, and in May 2016, further streamlined its smartphone hardware business, aligning with a strategy to create a vibrant Windows ecosystem with consistent experiences across first-party and OEM devices, focusing on narrower customer categories and differentiating through hardware and software integration. This shift led to reduced units sold and associated expenses in fiscal year 2016, a trend expected to continue in fiscal year 2017. The industry is dynamic and highly competitive, with frequent technological and business model changes, prompting Microsoft to invest in research and development to meet evolving customer demands and competitive pressures. Microsoft’s success depends on attracting and retaining qualified employees globally, offering competitive compensation, benefits, career growth opportunities, and a strong working environment. Revenue is significantly influenced by global macroeconomic and geopolitical factors, and international operations account for a large portion of total revenue and expenses, with foreign exchange rate fluctuations impacting reported revenue and expenses. The strengthening of the U.S. dollar relative to certain foreign currencies during fiscal years 2015 and 2016 negatively affected revenue and reduced expenses from international operations. Revenue historically fluctuates quarterly, with the second quarter typically being the highest due to year-end corporate spending and holiday consumer spending. Revenue deferral occurs for Windows 10 licenses, reflecting ratable recognition over the device’s life, and for bundled products and services. When customers opt for cloud-based versions instead of transactional products, revenue is recognized over subscription periods or upon consumption. Product revenue includes sales of operating systems, cross-device productivity applications, server and business applications, desktop and server management tools, software development tools, video games, hardware such as PCs, tablets, gaming consoles, phones, and related accessories, as well as training and certification. Service and other revenue includes cloud-based solutions like Office 365, Azure, Dynamics CRM Online, and Xbox Live, solution support, consulting, and online advertising. Microsoft reports financial performance through three reportable segments—Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, and More Personal Computing—aligned with its strategic direction, beginning in fiscal year 2016. In June 2015, Microsoft restructured its organization to align with its strategy as a productivity and platform company. The chief operating decision maker, also the CEO, requested changes to the financial information reviewed for resource allocation and performance assessment, leading to the new segment reporting structure. Financial performance for LinkedIn is expected to be reported under the Productivity and Business Processes segment.
